title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Tool‑Augmented Agent vs LLM‑Only Generation for Intent‑Driven Network Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id: cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) evaluating whether augmenting an LLM with a deterministic NetOps verifier and a lightweight topology simulator (a tool‑augmented guarded pipeline) increases deterministic‑validator pass rates versus an LLM‑only baseline on intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered design used shared_initial_candidate semantics (a single LLM generation reused across both conditions). Planned n=300 paired tasks; 299 complete analyzable pairs. Observed deterministic‑validator passes: baseline 299/299, guarded 299/299 (contingency n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). Paired difference = 0.00 (McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], 10k resamples, seed=1729). Because the run reused identical LLM outputs across conditions, the experiment measures downstream verifier/tool processing of shared candidates rather than whether tool‑augmented agents produce different or safer independent generations. All artifacts, raw responses, validator traces, execution logs, and SHA‑256 hashes are archived (see Disclosure). We report exact contingency counts, deterministic reconciliation, and the preregistered sensitivity analyses; we document two technical failures and explain implications for inference and follow‑up designs (independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model replication, richer simulation).

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are being explored to translate operator intent into low‑level network device configurations (intent→config). Such outputs can be operationally unsafe unless checked by deterministic validators and simulators. We preregistered a paired confirmatory experiment to test the operational effect of adding a deterministic verifier and a lightweight topology simulator to an LLM pipeline. Crucially, the executed, preregistered generation semantics for this run were shared_initial_candidate: a single LLM generation was produced and reused for both the baseline (LLM‑only) and the guarded (tool‑augmented) conditions. The research question executed and answered by the archived run is therefore: given identical LLM candidate outputs, does downstream tool‑augmentation (deterministic validator + simulator) change deterministic‑validator pass/fail outcomes? This paper reports the preregistration, the frozen analysis plan, the execution manifest, deterministic reconciliation, and the exact numeric outcomes and artifacts supporting them.
sections.related_work: Prior work studies intent‑driven configuration, generate–validate–repair flows, and tool‑augmented agents for operational safety in NetOps [Nguyen Tu et al., 2024; PreConfig (arXiv:2403.09369); practical tool/runtime reliability reports and "verifier" analyses]. Ensembling, verifier‑tax tradeoffs, and runtime tool‑control policies have been proposed to improve agentic reliability. Our contribution is a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired study with explicit generation semantics and full SHA‑256‑backed provenance; the experimental contrast here is downstream verifier/tool processing under identical LLM outputs, which is a narrower but reproducible operational question than independent per‑condition generation comparisons.
sections.methodology: Preregistration. We froze a machine‑readable preregistration (study_id cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1; SHA‑256: 991674d5...) before execution that specified the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on deterministic‑validator pass), sampling plan (300 paired tasks; 150 simple/150 complex), validator, model provider, seeds, retry policy, and generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate). The full preregistration and its JSON fields are archived in the execution bundle.Path and tools. Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Declared LLM: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; hash recorded). Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0). The task bank used deterministic synthetic topology templates encoding initial and expected final states, allowed fields, and workflow constraints (e.g., shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break). Execution logging, raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, and full SHA‑256 hashes were recorded (execution_manifest; hash manifest).Design choices and their meaning. The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (explicit in preregistration and executed manifest) means: for each paired task a single LLM generation was produced and then fed (unchanged) into both the baseline and guarded scoring/validator pipelines. This isolates downstream verifier/tool processing from generation variance but precludes inference about whether independent tool‑augmented generation would produce different outputs. Statistical plan. Primary test: McNemar exact two‑sided on paired binary pass/fail; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10k resamples, seed=1729). Sensitivity analyses (preregistered) treat technical failures as verifier‑failures; multiplicity adjustments were not applied to exploratory analyses. Reproducibility. All raw artifacts and analysis scripts are archived; authoritative counts are in deterministic_reconciliation.json.
sections.results: Execution accounting. Planned episodes: 600 (300 pairs). Completed: 598 episodes; failed episodes: 2 (both constituting a single missing pair). Complete analyzable pairs: 299 (deterministic_reconciliation.json). Primary confirmatory outcome. Deterministic validator pass counts: baseline 299/299, guarded 299/299. Paired contingency (complete pairs): n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Paired difference (guarded−baseline)=0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap (10k, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI for paired difference = [0.00, 0.00]. Interpretation constraint. Because both conditions saw identical generated artifacts by design, the observed null paired difference is an artifact‑grounded, correct answer to the executed estimand (effect of downstream tooling on a shared set of LLM candidates). It is not evidence about whether independent per‑condition tool‑augmented generation would produce safer outputs. Power and ceiling effect. The preregistered power calculation assumed a baseline pass ≈0.60 and targeted a 0.20 absolute paired‑difference with n=300. The observed baseline success rate was 1.00 (299/299), violating the power assumption and producing a ceiling effect: the originally powered contrast is therefore uninformative for detecting the predeclared minimally important effect in this run. Missingness and failures. One paired item was missing (both episodes failed). The missing pair identifier is pair-000269 (episodes task-000269-baseline and task-000269-guarded are absent from the response artifact set). Detailed per‑episode failure records (provider error codes, timestamps, and low‑level logs) are recorded in execution/execution_log.jsonl (artifact SHA‑256: b45a600859502b088a9416744ccbff3f5fba2e6dd76b863440bdfd36ebf21bb8) and in the provider call traces (execution/provider_calls/*; manifest includes sha256 values). Deterministic reconciliation. The deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms completed_episode_count=598, failed_episode_count=2, complete_pair_count=299, and provider_call audit (hosted_model_call_event_count=300, completed=299, failed=1). Representative artifacts. Representative scoring JSONs and validator traces are archived and example scoring entries (task‑000001, task‑000002, task‑000003) are included in the evidence bundle (execution/scoring/*.json; hashes recorded).
sections.discussion: What this run shows. Under the preregistered, executed protocol (shared_initial_candidate), downstream tool‑augmentation did not change deterministic‑validator pass outcomes for the shared candidate set: both pipelines accepted the same candidates in the analyzed confirmatory set. This is a reliable, reproducible factual outcome anchored to the archived artifacts. What this run does not show. It does not answer whether an agentic, tool‑augmented system that is permitted to generate its own candidates per condition would produce different or safer generations; that remains an open, preregistered follow‑up question. Methodological implications. Shared_initial_candidate is a defensible design choice when the scientific aim is to isolate downstream verifier/tool processing; but it reduces sensitivity to generation‑level improvements and can create ceiling effects if the LLM produces high‑quality candidates for the chosen task bank. For claims about agentic generation, future confirmatory preregistrations should (a) switch to independent per‑condition generation semantics, (b) increase sample size or presence of harder tasks to avoid ceiling rates, and (c) account for increased model‑call budgets and variance. Validator construct validity. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces syntactic parsing, per‑interface field checks, dependency/workflow rules (make_before_break, shutdown_configure_restore, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change), and reachability‑style invariants simulated by the lightweight topology simulator. A concise, artifact‑anchored description of the validator rules and unit tests is available in execution/transformation_manifest.json (hash fb93ea7f...) and in the validator scoring JSONs; these artifacts show exact violation codes and representative rule checks. Operational lesson. Deterministic validators produce traceable, debuggable outputs (parsed_command_count, final_state snapshots, violation codes) which are valuable even when generation quality is high; they support auditability, post‑hoc failure analysis, and transparent reproducibility. Limitations and external validity. Tasks were synthetic and evaluated with a lightweight simulator; results do not generalize to vendor‑rich CLIs, production telemetry, or other LLM families. Single model (declared gpt‑5‑mini) was used; multi‑model replication is needed for external claims. Two technical failures occurred (pair‑000269); detailed logs are in execution_log.jsonl (SHA256 b45a6008...).
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired study that asked: given identical LLM candidates (shared_initial_candidate), does downstream tool‑augmentation change deterministic‑validator pass rates? For the 299 analyzable pairs the answer was no: both baseline and guarded pipelines accepted the same candidates (299/299 each). That empirical fact is reproducible from the archived artifacts. The design choice to reuse a shared initial candidate is central to interpreting this outcome: it isolates downstream processing but prevents conclusions about agentic generation benefits. We therefore recommend two concrete next steps for the community: (1) preregister and run an independent per‑condition generation paired trial (larger sample and multi‑model) to evaluate agentic generation effects; (2) replicate with richer vendor CLIs and simulators to improve external validity. All raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, and SHA‑256 hashes are archived and provided in the execution manifest to enable independent verification and reanalysis.

limitations: The preregistered execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (single LLM generation reused across baseline and guarded). That design makes this run an assessment of downstream verifier/tool effects given identical generated artifacts, and it precludes inference about whether tool‑augmented agents produce safer independent generations.
Tasks were synthetic and evaluated in a lightweight simulator; external validity to heterogeneous vendor CLIs, complex runtime state, and production NetOps telemetry is limited.
Only a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) was exercised; results do not generalize across model families or sizes.
The deterministic validator approximates operational checks but cannot capture all real runtime side effects or hardware/software heterogeneity.

Because both conditions observed identical generated artifacts in the confirmatory set, the primary statistical test is insensitive to generation‑level effects and cannot settle broader claims about agentic generation benefits.
